newsitem.title: INDIA: Indians welcome budget tax cuts but smokers glum.
newsitem.headline: Indians welcome budget tax cuts but smokers glum.

text.p: Many people in India's commercial capital of Bombay on Saturday welcomed lower rates of income-tax in the budget for financial 1997/98 (April-March), but higher duties on cigarettes wiped the smile from smokers' faces.
"We have been hoping for something like this for a long time. I'm very happy because I hate giving away my salary to the government," said Harish Sheth, a 28-year-old advertising executive.

Indian Finance Minister P. Chidambaram on Friday slashed personal rates of income-tax by ten percentage points across the board in his second budget, saying he believed moderate rates of personal income-tax would help reduce tax evasion.

India's wage-earning middle-class, estimated to be over 200 million strong, watches the tax proposals in the budget very closely every year. An estimated 12 million Indians -- both firms and individuals -- pay income-tax, official figures show.

But a snap poll showed many people were unhappy with another scheme Chidambaram has thought up to enforce compliance. He has proposed that anyone owning a home, a car, or a telephone be mandatorily required to file an income-tax return.

"He's taking away with one hand what he gives with another," said Anand Sharma, a bank clerk. "Basically he wants to tax the same tiny group of salaried tax-payers in as many different ways as possible."
India, with a population of 930 million, has one telephone for every 100 people, and more than 3.3 million cars, taxis and jeeps at last count in 1993.

This last figure is increasing by about 300,000 cars annually, propelled by a transforming economy that has seen many ambitious young white-collar workers buying international makes for the first time.

"I am happy that the Finance Minister has reduced the tax slab for pensioners," said Arvind Nayak, 63, who retired from a job with a multinational chemicals firm recently. "It means that I won't have to worry so much about saving."
Like Nayak, many retired people have had to watch helplessly as inflation, currently rising at the rate of around seven percent, against five percent last year, erodes the value of their savings.
Smokers fell victim to Chidambaram's zeal to stamp out the threat from cancer.

"The fight against cancer and respiratory diseases continues," Chidambaram told parliament while presenting the budget. "My contribution will be to increase the excise duty on non-filter cigarettes... and other categories of cigarettes."
But he left virtually untouched the excise structure on the harsh cheerot-like rolled leaf "beedi", which thousands of poor Indians smoke.
"If the finance minister was serious about it, he would have raised the taxes on both cigarettes and "beedis" equally," said smoker and engineering student, Anita Zaveri, 18.
"By targeting only cigarettes, he is driving people to smoke 'beedis', which are actually worse," Zaveri added.
